extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; creative writers interested in heroic/poetic greatness
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging Great Men (heroes, poets, priests, reformers) with focus on poets like Dante and Shakespeare — what makes their greatness: vision, morality, universality, craft, and authenticity. Useful for literary criticism or creative writers aiming for enduring work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not judged by worldly effect or utility
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is not by what is called their effect on the world, by what _we_ can judge of their effect there, that a man and his work are measured. Effect? Influence? Utility?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate greatness with visible influence, political success, or utility. Carlyle argues that the real fruit of a man's work may be unrelated to immediate worldly consequences (example: Mahomet's worldly empire vs Dante's nobler, more lasting voice). Evaluate intrinsic quality, profundity, and inner significance rather than mere public impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of silence and unseen fruit
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let us honor the great empire of _Silence_, once more! The boundless treasury which we do not jingle in our pockets… It is perhaps, of all things, the usefulest for each of us to do, in these loud times.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and prize quiet, unadvertised creative depth and influence. Enduring artistic worth may grow silently and need not be loud, immediate, or celebrated in its own time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment of a culture's inner or outer life
rubrics_metrics.description: “As Dante…was sent…to embody musically the Religion of the Middle Ages, …so Shakspeare…embodies for us the Outer Life of our Europe… Dante has given us the Faith or soul; Shakspeare… has given us the Practice or body.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a writer successfully embodies fundamental aspects of an age (its inner spiritual life or its social/outer practices). A great poet can stand as the living representation of a culture's soul or body.

rubrics_metrics.name: The seeing eye (vision) — primary poetic gift
rubrics_metrics.description: “To the Poet, as to every other, we say first of all, _See_. If you cannot do that, it is of no use to keep stringing rhymes together…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fundamental criterion is the ability to 'see' — to discern the inner heart, harmony, and essential truth of things. Evaluate whether the work reveals penetrating perception rather than mere surface ornament or verbal skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of vision as a measure of greatness (superiority of intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: “For, in fact, I say the degree of vision that dwells in a man is a correct measure of the man. If called to define Shakspeare's faculty, I should say superiority of Intellect…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the depth and breadth of intellectual insight — unity of imagination, fancy, understanding — as central to greatness. The fitter and more comprehensive the understanding, the better the creative response will be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to make order out of chaos (‘Fiat lux’)
rubrics_metrics.description: “To find out this, you task the whole force of insight that is in the man. … Can the man say, _Fiat lux_, Let there be light; and out of chaos make a world?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the creator’s power to discern structure: to select beginnings, order events, and produce coherent narrative or argument from confusion. Artistic mastery includes the capacity to impose illuminating form on disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait-painting / delineation of men (characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is in what I called Portrait-painting, delineating of men and things, especially of men, that Shakspeare is great. All the greatness of the man comes out decisively here.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fidelity and depth of character depiction: whether characters are shown in 'their inmost heart' and with generic, structural truth. Great characterization makes inner mechanisms visible and universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral quality integral to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Without morality, intellect were impossible for him; a thoroughly immoral _man_ could not know anything at all! To know a thing… a man must first _love_ the thing, sympathize with it: that is, be _virtuously_ related to it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the author's ethical relation to subject-matter: justice, courage, and sympathy enrich insight. Carlyle claims moral virtue is a precondition for deep knowing — evaluate whether the work springs from a just and courageous engagement with its material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / art that is not artifice (unconscious origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Shakspeare's Art is not Artifice; the noblest worth of it is not there by plan or precontrivance. It grows up from the deeps of Nature, through this noble sincere soul…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that feel organically grown from inner necessity rather than contrived cleverness. Authentic, 'unconscious' creation — emergence from 'deeps' of the artist — signals higher artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perenniality and capacity to yield new meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: “The latest generations of men will find new meanings in Shakspeare… 'new harmonies with the infinite structure of the Universe; concurrences with later ideas …'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work can be re-read across ages and still yield fresh insights. Enduring works resonate with later sensibilities and continue to illuminate new contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth beneath speech — hidden roots and silence
rubrics_metrics.description: “How much in Shakspeare lies hid; his sorrows, his silent struggles known to himself; much that was not known at all… like _roots_, like sap and forces working underground! Speech is great; but Silence is greater.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appraise the subterranean complexity and unspoken reserves in a work — layers that imply depth beyond explicit expression. A mature work carries tacit depths that reward contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine, genial laughter (sympathetic humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: “And then, if not always the finest, it is always a genial laughter. Not at mere weakness, at misery or poverty; never. … Laughter means sympathy; good laughter is not 'the crackling of thorns under the pot.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the tone of humor: it should be sympathetic and humanizing rather than cruel or merely cynical. Laughter that enlarges sympathy indicates moral and artistic maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of construction / fitting of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: “The built house seems all so fit,--every way as it should be, as if it came there by its own law and the nature of things,--we forget the rude disorderly quarry it was shaped from. The very perfection of the house… hides the builder's merit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate technical craft: unity, fitness of form to material, and the seamlessness of structure. Mastery often conceals labor; a work that appears 'natural' and perfectly proportioned indicates high skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and universality (true catholicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We may call Shakspeare the still more melodious Priest of a _true_ Catholicism,… not unfit to make itself heard among the still more sacred Psalms. … neither narrow superstition, harsh asceticism, intolerance…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work manifests a sincere, inclusive humanism that embraces a broad, universal vision rather than sectarian narrowness. Universal sympathy and tolerance are marks of a great poet-priest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity over rhetorically conscious 'prophethood'
rubrics_metrics.description: “And, at bottom, was it not perhaps far better that this Shakspeare … was _conscious_ of no Heavenly message? He did not feel… that he specially was the 'Prophet of God.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer authenticity over self-conscious missionary rhetoric: greatness may be greater when unconscious of grandiose claims. Avoid conflating fervor of rhetoric with genuine magnitude of vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to articulate national/cultural identity
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a great thing for a Nation that it get an articulate voice; that it produce a man who will speak forth melodiously what the heart of it means!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether an author furnishes an enduring voice that can unify or express a people's sensibility across time and space. Such cultural articulation can be counted as a form of greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-aware judgment — works formed by conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Alas, Shakspeare had to write for the Globe Playhouse: his great soul had to crush itself, as it could, into that and no other mould. It was with him, then, as it is with us all. No man works save under conditions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in circumstances and constraints of production when evaluating a work. Fragments or 'disjecta membra' may represent a greater whole curtailed by historical or material limits; judge both aspiration and realized product.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Reformer-as-Priest criterion (spiritual conviction for social change)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Is not every true Reformer, by the nature of him, a _Priest_ first of all? He appeals to Heaven's invisible justice against Earth's visible force;… He is a believer in the divine truth of things; a _seer_…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reformist or prophetic writing/actors, look for spiritual conviction, seership, and appeal to higher justice rather than mere political maneuvering. Effective reform requires priestly moral and visionary authority.
